solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dicky waits round university for dance (6)

indicators.note: dicky means shaky or unsound, so the letters are out of order
the anagrammed letters go round the U

annotation.surface: Nervous waiters hover around a college dance, hoping for a turn on the floor.
annotation.walkthrough: Dicky is British slang for weak or unreliable, as in a dicky heart. The U is folded into the shuffle, so all six letters rearrange together.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Watusi was one of the early-1960s craze dances, alongside the Twist.

clue.text: Who’s beginning to anticipate a new Ring in development? (9)

definitions.text: Who’s beginning to anticipate a new Ring in development?

indicators.note: takes the first letter of anticipate
something developing changes shape, so the letters rearrange

annotation.surface: An opera fan waits eagerly for a new production of the Ring cycle.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a Wagner devotee is exactly who looks forward to a new staging of the Ring, his four-opera cycle.
annotation.definitionFit: A Wagnerian is an admirer of Wagner, composer of the Ring.

clue.text: Excerpt from Rigoletto stirred composer (5)

indicators.note: an excerpt is a piece lifted out of a longer text

annotation.surface: A passage from Verdi's Rigoletto moved a composer in the audience.
annotation.walkthrough: The opera setting points toward Verdi, but the hidden answer is Paolo Tosti, a late Victorian writer of drawing-room songs.
annotation.definitionFit: Francesco Paolo Tosti was an Italian composer of popular songs.

clue.text: Drink salesmen turning up outside hotel (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the word from the bottom
the first piece goes round the second

annotation.surface: Travelling salesmen arrive for a drink outside their hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: The reversal comes first and the hotel goes inside afterwards. The Ritz is the crossword's standard hotel.
annotation.definitionFit: A spritzer is a drink of wine and soda water.

clue.text: Teacher turned offensive when bored by Roman statesman (8)

indicators.note: turned round, so read backwards
something bored has another piece drilled into it

blocks.note: Cato, censor of the Roman Republic

annotation.surface: A teacher turned nasty because a lesson on a Roman statesman bored him.
annotation.walkthrough: Bored reads as tedium in the surface; in the wordplay it means drilled, with CATO driven into EDUR.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name someone whose job is to instruct others.

clue.text: Deceit upped London borough by 100 per cent (6-7)

blocks.note: read with 'by 100 per cent', which comes after the borough
raising something by 100 per cent doubles it
Ealing, a borough in west London

annotation.surface: A fraud scandal in which a London council's figures were inflated twofold.
annotation.walkthrough: The D of DOUBLED is shared across the hyphen: DOUBLED + EALING reads DOUBLE-DEALING.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: acting one way while intending another is deceit.

clue.text: What’s about in our land that bird call introduces? (6)

definitions.text: What’s about in our land that bird call introduces?

indicators.note: 'about in our land' places the first piece within the second, as a person is in a country
the call has the other letters introduced into it

blocks.note: the setter's land, the United Kingdom

annotation.surface: A question about which bird is heard in Britain, announcing itself by its call.
annotation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: about goes into our land, and that pair goes into the call. Read straight, the whole clue describes the bird, a spring visitor to Britain named after its own call.
annotation.definitionFit: The cuckoo is about in Britain in spring and is named for the call it makes.

clue.text: Rage engulfs business circle in Black Sea port once (9)

indicators.note: the outer word swallows the others

annotation.surface: Business anger boils over in an old Black Sea trading town.
annotation.walkthrough: Rage looks like anger but is a craze, as in all the rage. Once flags that the name is historical.
annotation.definitionFit: Trebizond is the old name of Trabzon, a Turkish port on the Black Sea.

clue.text: Billions lost from local railway station in Australia (5)

indicators.note: the B is taken away from the word

blocks.note: a branch line is a local railway

annotation.surface: Billions have been cut from a local railway line.
annotation.walkthrough: Station is a railway word in the surface, but in Australia a station is a large sheep or cattle farm.
annotation.definitionFit: A ranch is a large livestock farm, what Australians call a station.

clue.text: Backing separate sink — it keeps things fresher (3,4)

indicators.note: going backwards, so read the letters in reverse

annotation.surface: Advice on plumbing in a separate sink to keep the kitchen smelling fresh.
annotation.walkthrough: Sink looks like the kitchen fitting, and a gas trap does belong under one, but here it is the verb. PART + SAG is read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A gas trap is the water-filled bend in a drain that stops sewer smells coming back up.

clue.text: A sly sycophant possibly who understands when person’s lying? (13)

indicators.note: the letters could possibly form something else

annotation.surface: A cunning flatterer who can always tell when someone is telling lies.
annotation.walkthrough: Lying means telling untruths in the surface but reclining in the definition: the patient on the analyst's couch.
annotation.definitionFit: A psychoanalyst interprets what a patient says while lying on the couch.

clue.text: Soiled article brought to pawnbroker (7)

blocks.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker

annotation.surface: A dirty item is taken to the pawnshop.
annotation.walkthrough: Article looks like a thing being pawned; it is the grammatical kind. Uncle for a pawnbroker is old British slang, perhaps from the pawned goods being 'at my uncle's'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something dirtied, with the answer also carrying a ritual sense of impurity.

clue.text: One in set following European writer (5)

indicators.note: 'one in set' puts the first piece inside the second, as a member is in a set
following means coming after, so European is placed first

blocks.note: a lot = a set of items, as at auction

annotation.surface: A member of a group following a European writer.
annotation.walkthrough: I goes into LOT, and the result follows E.
annotation.definitionFit: George Eliot and T S Eliot are both writers.

clue.text: What was the Left? Rather mean and a bit cowardly? (9)

blocks.note: ye is an old spelling of the, as in Ye Olde Shoppe

annotation.surface: A political question: was the old Left a bit petty and a bit spineless?
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark hides the split after the: What was the gives YE, and Left is just L. Yellow means cowardly, so yellowish is a bit cowardly.
annotation.definitionFit: Yellow means cowardly, so yellowish is somewhat cowardly.

clue.text: Overlooked point he’s had emphasised to some extent (2,3,5)

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used

annotation.surface: Someone complains that a point they stressed was ignored to a degree.
annotation.walkthrough: Overlooked sits naturally with a point being ignored, which keeps it from looking like the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone left in another's shadow is outshone and so ignored.

clue.text: Deal mostly with less dubious accountant? (9)

indicators.note: most of the word, dropping its last letter

blocks.note: to treat = to deal (with), minus its last T

annotation.surface: Someone would rather deal with an accountant who is less shady.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks accountant as a slightly loose definition: a treasurer keeps an organisation's accounts.
annotation.definitionFit: A treasurer manages and accounts for an organisation's funds.

clue.text: Baby boomer‘s delight consuming Ecstasy (4)

indicators.note: the outer word eats the E

annotation.surface: A baby boomer's pleasure in taking ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: Baby boomer suggests someone born after the war, but a boomer is a male kangaroo, and its baby is a joey.
annotation.definitionFit: A joey is a young kangaroo, and a boomer is an adult male kangaroo.

clue.text: More than one American garden parasite produces scale (9)

blocks.note: Americans call a garden a yard
a tick is a blood-sucking parasite

annotation.surface: A garden pest spreading across American backyards.
annotation.walkthrough: Scale looks like a pest's skin or the scale insect, but here it is a standard of measurement.
annotation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a standard or scale by which things are measured.

clue.text: Trafficked mammal’s long suffering during distress (8)

indicators.note: the word is damaged, so its letters are rearranged
the scrambled letters go inside the other word

annotation.surface: A smuggled animal has suffered for a long time in misery.
annotation.walkthrough: Long suffering reads as one phrase, but it splits: long is the fodder and suffering scrambles it before it goes inside.
annotation.definitionFit: The pangolin, a scaly anteater, is among the most trafficked mammals in the world.

clue.text: A Christmas Carol — heartless story (4)

indicators.note: the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: a novel is a story; its heart is the middle letter V

annotation.surface: A verdict on Dickens's A Christmas Carol: a tale without feeling.
annotation.walkthrough: The title of Dickens's book looks like the subject of a review; it is really the definition, with the capitals only for show.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym: noel, from French Noël, is an old word for a carol sung at Christmas.

clue.text: Liver in flames looking bloody unfortunately flipped when chap’s interrupted (10)

indicators.note: turned over, so read backwards
MAN breaks into the reversed letters

annotation.surface: A chap with a bloodshot liver, a sorry sight, being turned over on the grill.
annotation.walkthrough: Liver means one who lives, not the organ: legend said the salamander could live in fire. The two pieces are joined before the flip, and only then does the chap break in.
annotation.definitionFit: In legend the salamander was a creature that could live in fire.

clue.text: Mother raised money as source of meal (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised reads the word from the bottom

annotation.surface: Mum scraped together money for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: Raised money reads as fundraising; here raised only turns COIN upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: Manioc, or cassava, is a root ground into meal and flour.

clue.text: An emperor overthrown by unusually fair religious follower (9)

indicators.note: turned over, so read backwards
the letters are arranged in an unusual order

annotation.surface: A deposed emperor is followed by a strangely just believer.
annotation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Rastafarians revere an emperor, Haile Selassie. A TSAR is read backwards, then FAIR is shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names an adherent of the Jamaican faith as well as the movement itself.

clue.text: Questionable degree in Afro-Cuban music (5)

annotation.surface: Doubts about a university qualification in Afro-Cuban music.
annotation.walkthrough: Rum is British slang for odd or suspicious, not the Caribbean drink the Cuban surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: The rumba is a dance and style of music from Cuba with African roots.

clue.text: A large number of birds without beak (5)

indicators.note: the named letters are taken away

annotation.surface: A big flock of birds that have lost their bills.
annotation.walkthrough: Beak is literal: the letters BEAK come out of GROSBEAKS.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific quantity standing for the general phrase: twelve dozen, 144, is a large number to count out.

clue.text: Social event smothered by everybody’s scent (5)

indicators.note: the first word is covered by the second

blocks.note: our = belonging to all of us

annotation.surface: A party where everyone's perfume is overpowering.
annotation.walkthrough: Do for a party is informal British usage, as in a leaving do.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean a smell, though scent leans pleasant and the other word less so.

clue.text: I’m forty — moving cause to feel humiliated (7)

indicators.note: things that are moving change position, so the letters shift out of the order given

annotation.surface: Turning forty is embarrassing.
annotation.walkthrough: Moving reads as emotional in the surface, but it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb once meant to subdue the flesh, and now means to shame deeply.

clue.text: Medal being presented by current Italian dramatist (7)

blocks.note: a play that is on is being presented

annotation.surface: An award is presented to a contemporary Italian playwright.
annotation.walkthrough: Current looks like an adjective, modern, but it is the physics symbol I.
annotation.definitionFit: Carlo Goldoni was an eighteenth-century Venetian playwright.

clue.text: Outrage at first of redevelopments to old urban centre (8)

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

blocks.note: a city is an urban centre

annotation.surface: Anger at the first stage of plans to redevelop an old town centre.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface outrage is a planning row; the definition is the stronger sense, a shocking act.
annotation.definitionFit: An atrocity is an outrage, a shockingly cruel act.

clue.text: A nerd or a kagoule? One of the two there will do! (6)

blocks.note: British slang for an obsessive, socially awkward enthusiast
a kagoule is a light hooded waterproof jacket

blocks.clueFragment: One of the two there will do!
blocks.note: surface padding: tells the solver either definition leads to the answer

annotation.surface: A question about which word fits, with the setter saying either will do.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain an anorak is an obsessive hobbyist, after the jackets worn by trainspotters. The tag tells you both definitions give the same answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Anorak means both a hooded waterproof jacket and, in British slang, a nerd.
